title: Al-Mujib, the Responsive
tomorrow: how wide does a heart have to be to make room for Kayla?

lines: A VOICE MEMO: PRAYING FOR YOU.
cards: A voice memo from someone's grandmother, a little too close to the phone: I'm praying for you, baby. Jordan's grandma sent one to Amira after hearing about the scholarship interview next week. Amira played it twice.
She typed thank you, deleted it, typed it again. Then she wondered: is that like du'a? Underneath sits a much older question.
When people ask God for something, is anyone listening, and does anyone answer?

teach.b: Islam's answer comes in a strikingly close-up verse of Surah Al-Baqarah: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me."
Look at what's missing. Nearby in the same surah, when people ask about the new moons, or what to spend, the answer begins: say.
Here there's no say. God answers directly. Near.
Elsewhere, the Qur'an says God is nearer to a person than their own jugular vein. That's today's Name: Al-Mujib, the Responsive, the one who answers. And the answer isn't always the thing asked for.

teach.h: NOW, SAVED, OR A HARM TURNED AWAY.
teach.b: A hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad says a du'a is answered in one of three ways: given now, saved for the hereafter, or a harm of the same size turned away.

teach.h: ASK, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN YOU.
teach.b: Jordan's grandmother's tradition says something close, in Jesus's words, from the King James Bible: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you."

The shared ground is real: both picture a God who wants to be asked, and who hears. The difference is real too. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells his followers to ask in his name, and Christians pray that way.
Muslims call on Allah directly, with no one between, because of that verse: I am near. Two houses, two ways of asking. And a grandmother in one of them praying for a girl from the other.

how: Alongside the five daily prayers, Muslims make du'a: personal requests to Allah in any language, at any time, sometimes with hands raised, trusting the promise of 2:186 that He is near and answers.

o: the Responsive, who hears and answers prayer
the one who grants every wish exactly
the one who replies only to the righteous

games.q: asking and answering — tap the pairs.
p: now, saved, or a harm turned away

s: in 2:186, God's answer begins with 'say', like the verses near it
here there's no 'say': God answers directly. I am nigh.
Jesus's words in Matthew picture a God who wants to be asked
"Ask, and it shall be given you" (Matthew 7:7, KJV).
a du'a that isn't granted right away wasn't heard
a hadith in Ahmad's Musnad names three answers: given now, saved for later, or a harm turned away.

games.q: your cousin asked God for months to get into one program, and didn't. 'du'a doesn't work,' he says. what does today's hadith offer him?
o: 'it may be answered now, saved for later, or as a harm turned away.'
'it only works if you use the exact right Arabic words.'
'if it wasn't given, it probably wasn't heard.'
games.why: the hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad names three ways a du'a is answered. 2:186 promises nearness and answer, not always the thing asked for.

practice: Grab a pen and write one thing you're asking for, in plain words, on a scrap of paper. If you pray, ask for it now in your own words, the way du'a is made, in any language.
Then fold the paper, and for the sit, rest your hand on it, and notice what it's like to have put it into words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mujib. The Responsive, near enough to answer with no one in between. Name forty-four.

orig.note: Arabic: the Responsive, the one who answers. 2:186: I answer the prayer of the suppliant.

carryVoice: The line for today: he answers, not always as asked, and never unheard. See you tomorrow.
